Where it began

David Gower was born in Tunbridge Wells on 1 April 1957, but he spent his early childhood in East Africa, where his father worked for the Colonial Service in Dar es Salaam. The family came home when David was six.

At prep school cricket became his favourite game, and a scholarship took him to The King's School, Canterbury, where he was in the first team at 14 and later its captain. Six months of law at University College London could not compete with the county game. He made his Leicestershire debut in 1975, and in that match a Lancashire batter called David Lloyd made a hundred against him. Years later the two would share a commentary box.

The player

Gower played 117 Tests for England between 1978 and 1992, scoring 8,231 runs at 44.25 with 18 hundreds and 39 fifties. He began in style. The very first ball he faced in Test cricket, against Pakistan at Edgbaston, he pulled for four.

His finest summer was 1985. As captain against Australia he made 166 at Trent Bridge, 215 at Edgbaston, his highest Test score, and 157 at The Oval. His 732 runs in the series came at 81.33, and England took the Ashes 3–1. In all he led England in 32 Tests, and in first-class cricket, for Leicestershire and then Hampshire, he made 26,339 runs.

What made him special

Above all, he was a joy to watch. A left-hander with a strong top hand and a light touch, he seemed to stroke the ball rather than hit it, and the word people reached for was graceful. He was a fine outfielder too, with brilliant catches and a hard, accurate throw.

The easy style had a flip side. Because he never looked hurried, some mistook calm for not caring, and a lovely cover drive and a thin edge could be close relations. Yet for long stretches the edges stayed away. At one point he went 119 Test innings in a row without a duck, a world record at the time.

Away from the middle

Later he became one of the best-liked voices in the game. From 1995 to 2003 he was a team captain on They Think It's All Over, the BBC comedy quiz. He presented Gower's Cricket Monthly and commentated for the BBC, for Channel Nine in Australia and, for many years, for Sky Sports, where colleagues called him Lord Gower.

He cared about the natural world too, and in 1989 he helped launch the World Land Trust with Gerald Durrell and David Attenborough. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, was made an OBE in 1992, entered the ICC Hall of Fame in 2009, and in 2018, for England's 1,000th Test, was picked in the country's greatest Test XI.

And finally

His Test bowling career came to a single wicket, at 16 runs apiece. So when he later put his name to a book called Can't Bat, Can't Bowl, Can't Field, the evidence of 8,231 runs and 74 catches suggested the title was, at most, one-third true.
